:::{#thm-moore-penrose-unique}
#### A matrix has at most one Moore-Penrose inverse

If $\matr{G}_1$ and $\matr{G}_2$ are both Moore-Penrose inverses
of an $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{A}$ (@def-moore-penrose),
then $\matr{G}_1 = \matr{G}_2$.

:::

::: proof

**$\matr{A} \matr{G}_1 = \matr{A} \matr{G}_2$.**

$$
\ba
\matr{A} \matr{G}_1
&= \tp{(\matr{A} \matr{G}_1)}
&& \text{(condition 3 for } \matr{G}_1 \text{)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{G}_1}\,\tp{\matr{A}}
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{G}_1}\,\tp{(\matr{A} \matr{G}_2 \matr{A})}
&& \text{(condition 1 for } \matr{G}_2 \text{)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{G}_1}\,\tp{\matr{A}}\,\tp{\matr{G}_2}\,\tp{\matr{A}}
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product, twice)}
\\
&= \tp{(\matr{A} \matr{G}_1)}\,\tp{(\matr{A} \matr{G}_2)}
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product, twice, and @thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= (\matr{A} \matr{G}_1)(\matr{A} \matr{G}_2)
&& \text{(condition 3 for } \matr{G}_1 \text{ and } \matr{G}_2 \text{)}
\\
&= (\matr{A} \matr{G}_1 \matr{A})\,\matr{G}_2
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{A} \matr{G}_2.
&& \text{(condition 1 for } \matr{G}_1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

**$\matr{G}_1 \matr{A} = \matr{G}_2 \matr{A}$.**

$$
\ba
\matr{G}_1 \matr{A}
&= \tp{(\matr{G}_1 \matr{A})}
&& \text{(condition 4 for } \matr{G}_1 \text{)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{A}}\,\tp{\matr{G}_1}
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product)}
\\
&= \tp{(\matr{A} \matr{G}_2 \matr{A})}\,\tp{\matr{G}_1}
&& \text{(condition 1 for } \matr{G}_2 \text{)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{A}}\,\tp{\matr{G}_2}\,\tp{\matr{A}}\,\tp{\matr{G}_1}
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product, twice)}
\\
&= \tp{(\matr{G}_2 \matr{A})}\,\tp{(\matr{G}_1 \matr{A})}
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product, twice, and @thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= (\matr{G}_2 \matr{A})(\matr{G}_1 \matr{A})
&& \text{(condition 4 for } \matr{G}_2 \text{ and } \matr{G}_1 \text{)}
\\
&= \matr{G}_2\,(\matr{A} \matr{G}_1 \matr{A})
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{G}_2 \matr{A}.
&& \text{(condition 1 for } \matr{G}_1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

**Conclusion.**

$$
\ba
\matr{G}_1
&= \matr{G}_1 \matr{A} \matr{G}_1
&& \text{(condition 2 for } \matr{G}_1 \text{)}
\\
&= \matr{G}_1\,(\matr{A} \matr{G}_2)
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc, and the first step)}
\\
&= (\matr{G}_1 \matr{A})\,\matr{G}_2
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= (\matr{G}_2 \matr{A})\,\matr{G}_2
&& \text{(the second step)}
\\
&= \matr{G}_2.
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc, and condition 2 for } \matr{G}_2 \text{)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-moore-penrose-unique}
#### Only one of the many generalized inverses qualifies

The matrix $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
has infinitely many generalized inverses
$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & g_{12} \\ g_{21} & g_{22} \end{bmatrix}$ (@exm-generalized-inverse),
and $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ is a Moore-Penrose inverse (@exm-moore-penrose).
By @thm-moore-penrose-unique it is the only one,
so every other choice of $g_{12}, g_{21}, g_{22}$ breaks condition 2, 3 or 4.
For instance, $g_{21} = 1$ (the rest $0$) gives
$\matr{G} \matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, which is not symmetric.

:::
